Based on the lessons learned at Colorado School of Mines, Rivium, and other early deployment sites, mitigating speed differentials between AVs and human-operated vehicles is critical. IRI could help mitigate this issue and simultaneously increase intersection safety for all roadway users. This harmonizes with recent U.S. Department of Transportation efforts in roadway digital infrastructure—the application of advanced sensing, computation, and communication to improve the efficiency and safety of roadway operations. In the application to AMDs, IRI would promote safe and sustained AV operating speeds within the flow of the surrounding conventional traffic with human-operated vehicles. It would also serve as a tool to observe system-level operations and performance, providing a common operating picture of the performance of AV fleets, and adherence to OMA policy and guidelines of operations. All of this would be in addition to the benefits that increased observability would have for traditional traffic management. The concept of IRI to augment and address the AV fleet operating environment for increased safety was recognized by SAE at an international conference as having technical substance worthy of inclusion in one of its journals for practices for advanced mobility (Lott, Young, and Zhu 2021). 35 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Over the last century, the evolution of transportation technology from the horse and buggy to the automobile has required the introduction of operations management to provide a means of giving direction to deconflict movements at roadway intersections. The process, commonly referred to as traffic signs and signals, is central to safe and efficient roadway use. Figure 20 illustrates initial operations management when the police officer at the intersection directed vehicles and how it has transitioned to the use of traffic signal systems. 1910 1970 Figure 20. Roadway intersection safety and operational management has evolved over the last 100 years from the human operator present at the intersection to the current use of traffic signal technology using colored signal lights that are often managed by moderately sophisticated control systems. A new generation of traffic control infrastructure will be required in the near to medium term to manage large-scale AV fleet deployments within AMDs. Figure 21 is a functional diagram illustrating the inputs, processing, and prospective application benefits of deploying this next generation of traffic control technology. The application of IRI will provide capabilities to do more than just govern the sequencing of traffic signals (red-yellow-green) to direct traffic movement. Using machine intelligence, complete 360° sensing and perception of all vehicles, people, and objects within an intersection at all times will be possible to direct and verify the safety and efficiency of the system, providing a complete feedback loop for the management of both traditional modes and AV fleets. Items on the left-hand side of Figure 21 represent the sensing technologies (or agents). The various sensor outputs are fused with connected vehicle data using artificial intelligence and machine learning located at the specific roadway intersection.
